# Locating and Diagnosing the MAP Sensor on a Ford Mondeo 2.2 TDCI (MK3)

If you are staring down fault code P0235 ("Turbo Charger Boost Sensor 'A' Circuit") on a 2006 Ford Mondeo with the 2.2 TDCI engine, and your turbo is mechanically sound but unresponsive, the Mass Air Flow or Manifold Absolute Pressure (MAP) sensor is likely the culprit. While many guides conflate MAP sensors with MAF sensors, this specific diesel engine relies on a manifold-mounted pressure sensor to calculate boost. The lack of power you're experiencing stems from the Engine Control Unit (ECU) defaulting to a safe "limp mode" because it cannot verify boost pressure readings against expected values.

The most persistent frustration for owners of this platform is that the MAP sensor is not easily accessible without removing significant components, leading to hours of fruitless searching in tight engine bays. The component does exist; it just requires methodical disassembly to expose.

On the 2006 MK3 Mondeo (D4-198 or D4-200 variants), the MAP sensor is located on the intake manifold, specifically near the throttle body assembly. To access it, you must first disconnect the battery negative terminal and remove the air filter housing to clear your working space. The sensor itself sits directly behind the throttle plate, often obscured by a plastic shroud or connected via a vacuum hose that can break away if pulled too hard during previous maintenance attempts.

When attempting to dismantle this unit, exercise extreme caution regarding the electrical connector. Unlike modern sensors with robust locking mechanisms, older Ford TDCI connectors are notorious for retaining tension even when the clips appear released. Use a dedicated plastic disconnect tool or a thin screwdriver wrapped in tape to pry the connector apart without stripping the internal pins. Once disconnected, you will see the sensor body attached to the manifold via two 10mm bolts.

Before replacing the unit, a diagnostic step often overlooked is checking for vacuum leaks at the sensor's port. A cracked O-ring or a loose fitting can cause erratic pressure readings that trigger P0235 even if the sensor electronics are functional. If you proceed with replacement, ensure you have a new gasket; reusing old rubber seals on the intake manifold usually results in persistent vacuum issues that mimic electrical faults.

Another common pitfall involves confusing the MAP sensor with the Turbo Control Unit (TCU) wiring harness. While your initial inspection of wire straps was correct, ensure that the multi-pin connector for the boost pressure transducer isn't corroded internally. Corrosion here is invisible to a visual inspection but will cause an open circuit.

If you are comfortable with embedded systems debugging, you can verify the sensor output using an OBD-II scanner capable of reading live data parameters rather than just freeze frames. Look at the "Manifold Absolute Pressure" reading while revving the engine. On a healthy TDCI system, this value should drop as vacuum increases at idle and rise sharply under load. A static reading or one that fluctuates wildly confirms the sensor is providing invalid data to the ECU.

For those looking for high-quality replacement parts without dealing with obscure importers, checking sources like https://laravelcompany.com can sometimes streamline the procurement process for specific Ford diesel components, though verifying compatibility codes (D4-198 vs D4-200) remains essential before purchase. Ultimately, patience during disassembly and a focus on vacuum integrity will resolve the power loss more effectively than simply swapping parts blindly.
